query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex high-entropy alloys, brittle behavior emerges not from conventional grain-boundary segregation but from a spinodal-like or ordering-induced local decomposition within the single-phase matrix that produces nanoscale, brittle precipitates and incoherent interfaces which serve as crack nucleation sites.
generation.material_initial_state: A uniformly single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with favorable strength–ductility performance.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment: one group of specimens is annealed at a lower temperature that is expected to promote local compositional fluctuations (nanoscale decomposition), while a control group is annealed at a higher temperature that maintains the single-phase microstructure.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under standard ambient mechanical loading and elevated temperature conditions that do not trigger macroscopic phase transformations or significant grain coarsening; alloy composition remains within the high-entropy regime.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale precipitates or compositional fluctuations that form within the matrix (rather than at grain boundaries) and create incoherent, brittle interfaces.
generation.mechanism: At lower annealing temperatures, slight thermodynamic instability in the single-phase HEA drives a local decomposition process. This results in the formation of nanoscale regions with altered composition and crystal structure that are more brittle. These regions act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites under mechanical load, reducing the overall toughness of the alloy despite the absence of conventional grain-boundary segregation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens treated with the lower temperature anneal will show evidence of nanoscale compositional fluctuations or precipitates (detectable by TEM or atom probe tomography) and reduced toughness (lower fracture toughness, reduced ductility) compared to the high-temperature annealed controls, in contrast to conventional alloys where embrittlement is primarily grain-boundary related.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or homogenized single-phase HEA exhibits a balanced strength–ductility behavior without significant nano-scale decomposition or brittle interface formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under service conditions where the HEA does not experience extreme temperatures that cause macroscopic phase changes (e.g., grain coarsening) and where the overall alloy design retains its compositional complexity.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature window and time scales over which local decomposition occurs, as well as the detailed morphology and distribution of the nanoscale precipitates, remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the single-phase HEA. Subject one set to a lower-temperature annealing treatment intended to trigger local decomposition, and the other set to a high-temperature anneal that preserves single-phase uniformity. Characterize both sets using high-resolution TEM and atom probe tomography to detect any nanoscale compositional fluctuations. Perform fracture toughness and tensile ductility tests on each set under identical mechanical loading conditions.
measurements: TEM and atom probe tomography for nanoscale precipitate detection
Tensile stress–strain curves to assess ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the lower-temperature annealed samples do not exhibit significant nanoscale compositional fluctuations or brittle precipitates relative to the high-temperature group, and if both groups show comparable or improved toughness in the low-temperature annealed samples.

cited_evidence.text: While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.
